name: Side-Channel & Microarchitectural Attacks
description: Timing, cache, power, EM, and speculative-execution (Spectre/Meltdown) side channels and defenses.

uss.narrative:
The earliest works in this list mark the watershed moment for microarchitectural security: the disclosure of transient-execution attacks. "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (USENIX 2018) showed that out-of-order execution lets an unprivileged process read protected kernel memory, shattering the assumption that hardware-enforced memory isolation was a hard boundary. The same year, "Foreshadow: Extracting the Keys to the Intel SGX Kingdom with Transient Out-of-Order Execution" (USENIX 2018) carried the idea into trusted execution environments, dumping SGX enclave secrets and sealing keys. Around them, a wave of more classical side-channel work matured: cache-protection bypasses via the TLB in "Translation Leak-aside Buffer" (USENIX 2018), the EM-based single-trace RSA recovery of "One&Done" (USENIX 2018), and the off-path Wi-Fi timing channel of "Off-Path TCP Exploit" (USENIX 2018) — together signaling that leakage could come from caches, TLBs, EM emanations, and network timing alike.

The following years shifted from discovery to systematization and defense, and from CPU caches to the whole microarchitecture. Defensive proposals like "ScatterCache: Thwarting Cache Attacks via Cache Set Randomization" (USENIX 2019) and the speculation-hardening of "DOLMA" (USENIX 2021) and "Swivel: Hardening WebAssembly against Spectre" (USENIX 2021) tried to close the channels, while attackers broadened the attack surface: "SPOILER" (USENIX 2019) linked speculative load hazards to Rowhammer, "Medusa" (USENIX 2020) automated MDS-style data sampling, and "Lord of the Ring(s)" (USENIX 2021) demonstrated contention on the CPU's on-chip ring interconnect — a channel beyond the cache hierarchy entirely. A recurring theme was automation and measurement of the leakage surface itself, exemplified by "Osiris: Automated Discovery of Microarchitectural Side Channels" (USENIX 2021). This period also saw the field cross into machine-learning targets, as "CSI NN" (USENIX 2019) reverse-engineered neural-network architectures over an EM side channel and "DeepHammer" (USENIX 2020) flipped DNN weight bits.

By the early 2020s the work turned to confidential computing, hardware mitigations, and the limits of vendor fixes. "CIPHERLEAKS" (USENIX 2021) broke constant-time crypto on AMD SEV through a ciphertext side channel, and "VoltPillager" (USENIX 2021) used hardware voltage glitching against SGX. Most strikingly, papers began defeating the very mitigations deployed after Spectre: "Branch History Injection" (USENIX 2022) and "RETBLEED: Arbitrary Speculative Code Execution with Return Instructions" (USENIX 2022) showed that hardware defenses against Spectre-v2 remained bypassable, while "ÆPIC Leak" (USENIX 2022) leaked uninitialized data architecturally rather than transiently.

The most recent listed work shows the area both diversifying and returning to fundamentals. New application domains appear, such as AR/VR keylogging from head motion in "Going through the motions" (USENIX 2023), even as core hardware threats persist — "ZenHammer: Rowhammer Attacks on AMD Zen-based Platforms" (USENIX 2024) extends Rowhammer to AMD's dominant Zen platforms. Across these venues the trajectory is clear: from a few headline transient-execution breaks, the field has grown into a mature discipline that systematically discovers channels (Osiris), broadens them beyond caches (ring interconnect, power, EM), repeatedly outpaces deployed mitigations (BHI, RETBLEED), and now contends with confidential-computing and emerging-platform threats while the underlying physics of leakage remains stubbornly hard to fully close.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this NDSS slice split cleanly into two camps. One camp treated Intel SGX enclaves as the thing to defend, building oblivious-access machinery so that even a privileged attacker watching memory could not infer what an enclave was doing — see "ZeroTrace: Oblivious Memory Primitives from Intel SGX" (NDSS 2018) and "OBLIVIATE: A Data Oblivious Filesystem for Intel SGX" (NDSS 2018). The other camp targeted everyday leakage: keystroke and input timing. "KeyDrown: Eliminating Software-Based Keystroke Timing Side-Channel Attacks" (NDSS 2018) and "JavaScript Zero: Real JavaScript and Zero Side-Channel Attacks" (NDSS 2018) tried to close browser and OS timing channels, while "Microarchitectural Minefields: 4K-Aliasing Covert Channel and Multi-Tenant Detection in IaaS Clouds" (NDSS 2018) mined the memory-order buffer for new covert channels in the cloud.

The Spectre and Meltdown disclosures reshaped the field almost immediately. NDSS work pivoted from cache-only leaks toward transient and speculative execution, first as a curiosity — "ExSpectre: Hiding Malware in Speculative Execution" (NDSS 2019) weaponized misprediction to hide code — and then as a systematic defense and detection problem. "ConTExT: A Generic Approach for Mitigating Spectre" (NDSS 2020) proposed a principled mitigation, while "Hunting the Haunter - Efficient Relational Symbolic Execution for Spectre with Haunted RelSE" (NDSS 2021), "SpecTaint: Speculative Taint Analysis for Discovering Spectre Gadgets" (NDSS 2021), and "Kasper: Scanning for Generalized Transient Execution Gadgets in the Linux Kernel" (NDSS 2022) turned gadget-hunting into an automated program-analysis discipline. In parallel, a whole physical-channel line grew up alongside the microarchitectural one: "Learning-based Practical Smartphone Eavesdropping with Built-in Accelerometer" (NDSS 2020) and "SurfingAttack" (NDSS 2020) showed sensors and ultrasound leaking or injecting speech, with "EarArray" (NDSS 2021) and "GhostTalk" (NDSS 2022) trading attack and defense over the same acoustic and power-line media.

By the mid-2020s the targets broadened again. Randomized-cache defenses like "PhantomCache: Obfuscating Cache Conflicts with Localized Randomization" (NDSS 2020) and Rowhammer hardening in "Copy-on-Flip: Hardening ECC Memory Against Rowhammer Attacks" (NDSS 2023) matured the defensive side, while attacks reached into new physical media and richer computation — electromagnetic leakage from cameras in "EM Eye" (NDSS 2024), idle-state power effects in "IdleLeak" (NDSS 2024), and VR keystroke inference from controller acoustics in "Eavesdropping on Controller Acoustic Emanation for Keystroke Inference Attack in Virtual Reality" (NDSS 2024). Confidential computing itself became a victim, as "CounterSEVeillance: Performance-Counter Attacks on AMD SEV-SNP" (NDSS 2025) turned hardware counters against the very TEEs the 2018 work had tried to protect.

The most recent NDSS 2026 papers show two frontiers. Machine learning is now both a target and a leak surface: "Shadow in the Cache: Unveiling and Mitigating Privacy Risks of KV-cache in LLM Inference" (NDSS 2026) and the closely related "I Know What You Asked: Prompt Leakage via KV-Cache Sharing in Multi-Tenant LLM Serving" (NDSS 2025) show shared LLM caches leaking prompts, while "DNN Latency Sequencing" (NDSS 2026) extracts model architectures from SGX enclaves via single-stepping. At the same time the classic microarchitectural hunt continues at ever finer granularity and in newer hardware — cross-VM leaks through "Exploiting TLBs in Virtualized GPUs for Cross-VM Side-Channel Attacks" (NDSS 2026), instruction-granularity branch-predictor attacks in "OCCUPY+PROBE" (NDSS 2026), hardware-fuzzing discovery of port contention in "PortRush" (NDSS 2026), revived page-cache attacks in "Eviction Notice" (NDSS 2026), and even remote network timing sharpened in "Time and Time Again: Leveraging TCP Timestamps to Improve Remote Timing Attacks" (NDSS 2026). The through-line is clear: what began as cache-and-enclave timing has become a general study of how every layer — silicon, sensors, clouds, and now AI serving stacks — leaks through the side.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this list, from IEEE S&P 2018, staked out how physical and memory-level effects could be weaponized against commodity systems. Papers like "FPGA-Based Remote Power Side-Channel Attacks" (S&P 2018) showed that shared silicon leaks power information even without physical probes, while the Rowhammer line — "Another Flip in the Wall of Rowhammer Defenses" (S&P 2018) and "Grand Pwning Unit: Accelerating Microarchitectural Attacks with the GPU" (S&P 2018) — demonstrated that attackers could keep flipping DRAM bits faster than defenders could patch. Alongside these hardware faults ran a quieter thread of sensor- and inference-based leakage, such as "EyeTell: Video-Assisted Touchscreen Keystroke Inference from Eye Movements" (S&P 2018).

The field's center of gravity shifted abruptly in 2019 with "Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution" (S&P 2019), which turned the CPU's own performance optimizations into a universal leakage primitive and set off a wave of transient-execution work — "RIDL: Rogue In-Flight Data Load" (S&P 2019) and later "CacheOut" and "CrossTalk" (both S&P 2021) mined ever-deeper microarchitectural buffers. In parallel, cache attacks matured into a science: "Theory and Practice of Finding Eviction Sets" (S&P 2019) and "Attack Directories, Not Caches" (S&P 2019) gave attackers principled tooling, while "Port Contention for Fun and Profit" (S&P 2019) exploited execution-port sharing on SMT cores.

By 2020-2022 the community pushed in two directions at once: broadening the attack surface and formalizing defense. New primitives arrived — "Plundervolt" (S&P 2020) and "PLATYPUS" (S&P 2021) turned voltage and power interfaces into software-only weapons, "LVI" (S&P 2020) reversed the Spectre model by injecting values into a victim, and Rowhammer evolved into "TRRespass" and "RAMBleed" (both S&P 2020) and its defense "ProTRR" (S&P 2022). At the same time, rigorous defenses emerged: "Spectector" (S&P 2020) and "Binsec/Rel" (S&P 2020) brought formal verification to speculative and constant-time leakage, and "Hardware-Software Contracts for Secure Speculation" (S&P 2021) proposed a shared abstraction for what hardware may leak. Confidential computing became a focal target, from "Racing in Hyperspace" (S&P 2018) hardening SGX to "A Systematic Look at Ciphertext Side Channels on AMD SEV-SNP" (S&P 2022).

The most recent S&P 2026 papers show the battle has moved squarely onto trusted execution environments and cloud isolation, now against far stronger baseline defenses. "TEE.Fail: Breaking Trusted Execution Environments via DDR5 Memory Bus Interposition" and "BreakFAST: Confused Deputy Attack on Infinity Fabric to Break AMD SEV-SNP" pierce the newest confidential-computing hardware, while "VMSCAPE" and "Rain: Transiently Leaking Data from Public Clouds Using Old Vulnerabilities" show that incomplete branch-predictor isolation and lingering transient-execution bugs still leak across virtualized cloud tenants. Defense has likewise grown more formal — "Goldilocks and the Three P-States" (S&P 2026) offers formal leakage guarantees against Hertzbleed-style remote timing, and "Interplay of Efficient Model Checking and Secure Processor Design" (S&P 2026) folds model checking into secure-speculation processor design — signaling a field that now pairs ever-more-physical attacks with provably grounded mitigations.

ccs.narrative:
Side-channel research at CCS underwent a step change in 2018-2019 with the disclosure of speculative-execution vulnerabilities. ret2spec: Speculative Execution Using Return Stack Buffers (CCS 2018) extended Spectre to return-stack-buffer misprediction, while Rendered Insecure: GPU Side Channel Attacks are Practical (CCS 2018) showed graphics workloads leak secrets via timing. Screaming Channels: When Electromagnetic Side Channels Meet Radio Transceivers (CCS 2018) discovered that RF transceivers broadcast digital computation side channels wirelessly.

The 2019 wave brought silicon-confirmed transient-execution attacks: ZombieLoad: Cross-Privilege-Boundary Data Sampling (CCS 2019) sampled values from CPU load buffers across privilege boundaries, Fallout: Leaking Data on Meltdown-resistant CPUs (CCS 2019) exploited the store buffer to bypass Meltdown mitigations, and SMoTherSpectre: Exploiting Speculative Execution through Port Contention (CCS 2019) leveraged execution-port pressure as an oracle. Nemesis: Studying Microarchitectural Timing Leaks in Rudimentary CPU Interrupt Logic (CCS 2018) exposed that enclave interrupt timing also leaks secrets.

Defense research followed in 2020-2021: InSpectre: Breaking and Fixing Microarchitectural Vulnerabilities by Formal Analysis (CCS 2020) used formal methods to both find and repair Spectre gadgets, and Constantine: Automatic Side-Channel Resistance Using Efficient Control and Data Flow Linearization (CCS 2021) automatically eliminated control and data-flow leakage from sensitive code paths.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list marks the moment side channels went from a specialized concern to a discipline-defining crisis. In 2018, Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space (USENIX 2018) showed that out-of-order execution could leak arbitrary kernel memory across the most basic isolation boundary, and Foreshadow (USENIX 2018) turned the same transient-execution trick against Intel SGX, extracting the enclave's attestation keys. Alongside these speculative attacks, the same year's venues covered the full spread of physical and microarchitectural channels: FPGA-Based Remote Power Side-Channel Attacks (S&P 2018) and Screaming Channels (CCS 2018) pushed power and EM leakage into remote and RF settings, Another Flip in the Wall of Rowhammer Defenses (S&P 2018) kept the DRAM bit-flipping arms race alive, and Rendered Insecure: GPU Side Channel Attacks are Practical (CCS 2018) plus Grand Pwning Unit (S&P 2018) opened the GPU as an attack surface.

The pivotal shift came with Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution (S&P 2019), which generalized Meltdown's insight into a whole family of branch-prediction attacks that no simple patch could close. This triggered a wave of "transient execution" research: ret2spec (CCS 2018) abused return stack buffers, while a cluster of 2019 papers — RIDL (S&P 2019), ZombieLoad (CCS 2019), and Fallout (CCS 2019) — showed that even Meltdown-resistant CPUs leaked data straight out of internal microarchitectural buffers (the MDS class). Attackers also mined subtler contention channels, as in Port Contention for Fun and Profit (S&P 2019) and SMoTherSpectre (CCS 2019). Defenders responded on two fronts: randomized cache designs like ScatterCache (USENIX 2019) and principled, formal detection of leaks with Spectector (S&P 2020).

By 2020-2022 the field broadened from pure information leakage into fault injection, DRAM integrity, and machine-learning targets. Plundervolt (S&P 2020) and PLATYPUS (S&P 2021) weaponized the CPU's own voltage and power interfaces from software, LVI (S&P 2020) inverted Spectre by injecting attacker values into a victim, and TRRespass (S&P 2020) plus RAMBleed (S&P 2020) defeated the newest Rowhammer mitigations and turned bit flips into a read primitive. A distinct thread aimed these tools at neural networks — CSI NN (USENIX 2019) reverse-engineered architectures over EM, DeepHammer (USENIX 2020) degraded models via targeted bit flips, and DeepSteal (S&P 2022) stole weights from memory — signaling that the "secret" being leaked was increasingly a proprietary model.

The most recent work, concentrated in NDSS 2026, shows the area both maturing and chasing new platforms. Classic channels are being revived and sharpened: Eviction Notice: Reviving and Advancing Page Cache Attacks and Time and Time Again: Leveraging TCP Timestamps to Improve Remote Timing Attacks refine long-standing techniques, while OCCUPY+PROBE and PortRush push branch-target-buffer and port-contention attacks to finer granularity and toward automated hardware fuzzing. At the same time the targets have shifted decisively toward accelerators and AI: Exploiting TLBs in Virtualized GPUs for Cross-VM Side-Channel Attacks and Side-channel Inference of User Activities in AR/VR Using GPU Profiling attack the GPU-heavy cloud and immersive computing, DNN Latency Sequencing extracts model architectures from SGX enclaves, and Shadow in the Cache: Unveiling and Mitigating Privacy Risks of KV-cache in LLM Inference brings the whole tradition to bear on large language models — a clear sign that side-channel research now follows wherever sensitive computation and shared hardware meet.
